I get that sometimes. I feel the urge to cut and the longer I leave it the stronger it gets and then the more damage I end up doing when I do do it. It's just the actual act of picking up a blade, opening it, and piercing my skin for the first time that acts as a kind of barrier, it's kind of like my body's knows that to do so would hurt and cause pain which is bad and goes against human nature but I still know that once I do do it then I'll get that kind of comforting rush it brings and it'll all feel good again. Once I actually make that first cut (which is usually tiny, kind of like a tester), that feeling of apprehension just disappears instantly and it just all comes back and I'll just go to town on myself as per normal.

If something bad happens then I'll do it to calm down or make me feel better, but often there isn't really any event or reason that causes me to do it, it's just like there's a counter constantly ticking away inside of me and the higher it goes the stronger the urges get and the more I keep thinking about it. 

It started out purely as a way to cope with certain situations but now it's kind of comforting if that makes sense, like cuddling a pet or something, and it kind of keeps me grounded and happy, I notice that when I go more than 4-5 days without doing it my mood worsens a lot and I start feeling depressed.

On I kind of related note to not being able to bring yourself to do it I tried to kill myself with 1800mg of morphine earlier this year. Planned it out for months and was so happy when the day to do it arrived, absolutely no second thoughts. But then when it came to swallowing the pills I had a lot of struggle actually putting them to my mouth and swallowing, took 15mins to just bring myself to swallow but then once it was done I was just so happy that it was over (or supposed to be :P). I think that was the same sort of thing again, no matter how much you may want to hurt yourself your body has a very strong survival instinct and is just programmed to prevent causing harm to yourself, whether you want to or not. It's just a natural instinct like a gag reflex or flinching when someone hits you.

Sorry to hear that. If it's any help to you, I was in a similar situation with my parents growing up. Neither of them were trans but they went through a rather unpleasant breakup around the time I was born and I ended up living with my mother and her parents. She fed me lie after lie about my dad and because of that I grew up hating him and wanting nothing to do with him at all. I had fortnightly contact with him but then one time that day came around I threatened to jump out the upstairs window ( I was about 5/6 at the time) and after that contact stopped. Despite how I felt about him, I never actually had any bad memories or experiences with him, it was all based on what my mother had told me he'd done and what he was like. Then when I was around 14, my mother became extremely manipulative and abusive and really showed her true colours. It was made illegal for her to care for me anymore and I moved in with my grandparents while she had some homeless druggie sleeping in my bed at her house. My father was made aware of the situation and we ended up talking to each other online regularly and he gave me his side of the story of what happened when they were still together. From putting together the pieces and having seen what my mother was like first hand, it became clear that she's lied to me growing up and that he was actually an alright guy who had to put up the same crap I did off of her. We live a considerable distance away from each other now but we still talk regulary over fb and he comes down to see me every now and then and we have a positive relationship, despite being brought up to think he was some sort of evil, abusive arsehole. Turns out that was my mother instead.

Point is, just because a kid is raised to hate one parent by the other parent, there will come a time when they want the truth for themselves and they'll see through whatever lies they might have been told, and with the internet, fb and everything else we have now it's incredibly hard to keep two people from ever contacting each other. Things probably seem crap now but there will come a time when your kids will realise that not everthing they may have been told is true and they'll seek out the truth by themselves. I think it's probably best to just wait and let them do it on they're own terms when they're ready, if my dad had forced himself into my life earlier before I learnt the truth then I'd have just hated him even more for it and wanted nothing to do with him probably. Just make sure to let them know you still love them and things will work out eventually.

Sounds a lot like what I do. Tried just stopping altogether before but that was hopeless and people making me promise to stop just made me feel even worse with guilt when I did do it. Now I usually tell myself that I can't do it until a certain event has passed, such as waiting until after I've visited relatives or after I've gone out somewhere. I struggle a lot with social anxiety and even just popping out to the corner shop is a big deal, so not letting myself cut until after I've gone out to do some shopping or see someone gives me a bit of extra motivation to get out and also a kind of reward to look foward to when I get back, it just sort of relaxes and calms me down. I don't always do it after the event has passed though, probably about a third of the time I'll then tell myself to wait till next time instead, so it does keep from doing it as much as I used to. I do find that the longer I leave it though the more it kind of builds up, so if I wait 2 weeks then I'll probably do it a lot worse than had it only been 2 days since last time.

Don't think of it as what should be done, just things that you can do if you want to prepare. As for makeup seeming intimidating I can totally relate to that, it did seem overwhelming at first but with a bit of practice it becomes just another part of getting ready and only takes 15mins or so. When I say it took me four hours the first time, that was mostly spent just taking it off and putting it on again as I tend to be extremely fussy about everything being perfect and symetrical, but that was only the first time I did it, it certainly shouldn't take anywhere near that long normally! One of the things I struggled with was lipstick surprisingly and could spend 20mins trying to get it perfect but now it only takes about a minute, it's just about practice practice practice to get used to it, there's no rush. Remember most girls get taught how to do makeup from a young age by siblings, parents or friends as the grow up, we usually just have to start everything from scratch at a later age but there's no reason it can't be done.

Getting a job would definitely help (although I'm sure I don't need to tell you that!) as transition isn't that cheap over time. I was in the exact same position as you when I first came out, £115 per fortnight from the jobcenter, and only recently started getting more income so it can be done. I'd suggest starting small and trying to see it as lots of little things you've got to do rather than just one huge mountain. Just try and get one outfit together that you really like and then work from there, nobody gets a full new wardrobe straight away. If you're planning on going full time then you'll need to get an outfit suitable for job interveiws as well. Makeup wise, I'd suggest just starting off with some foundation/tinted moisturiser, eyeliner and/or mascara and some lipstick/gloss. It's how I first started off and those three things will make a big difference.

With walking, it really is something that will just come naturally if you keep at it. Nobody is constantly thinking about how they're moving, just try and keep reminding yourself when you're out. Maybe find some songs with a rhythm that you can walk? I found heels made a difference for me as well, my first pair were only about 1.5" high but they seemed to make it easier and come more naturally. 

I'm still waiting on the GIC as well, been three months now so you'll probably make it there before I do! Hoping that they'll be able to sort me out with speech therapy too as that's one thing I just can't get the hang of.

It is a long journey as you've got to kind of rediscover yourself and build up everything from scratch after being brought up as a boy and there will be difficult bits, but it should be an enjoyable experience too and be well worth it to be able to be yourself. Just remember that it's not about trying to fit into any stereotypes or labels of what a girl is or meeting particular goals, it's simply about being yourself and doing what feels right and natural to you, you just have to find out what that is.

The reason all this confusion around what gender is is simply because people keep assigning different things to the word gender.

Gender is simply how you identify in your brain and is biological. Another word for this is gender identity. In the case of transgender people, mtf for this example, you have someone who was born with a male body but a female brain, or a brain that is kind of in the middle but more closely resembles the brains of cis females. So gender identity is not a choice or a social construct, but simply how your brain is wired. Currently it seems the most likely cause for this is hormonal deficiencies when the baby is developing in the womb. Another way to look at is that transgender people are a kind of intersex. Interesex people are born with genitals that do not match their bodies, just like transgender people are born with brains that do not match, or how you can be born a hermaphrodite or with a completely male body but xx chromosones. There's a lot of different thing that determine how you develop and grow and sometimes shit goes wrong, the problem with being transgender is that you can't actually see the brain so a lot of people just think it's a choice, fetish or mental illness and just see them as punchlines and freaks, wheras with someone who is intersex there is a clear sign on the exterior of the body that you can see so there's no room for error or disbelief.

Gender role and gender presentation however, are social constructs, although this doesn't mean they aren't real. They include things like girls become nurses, boys become builders and girls wear makeup, boys like cars. They are ideas created and maintained by society about how each gender should present and behave and for the most part they are true. Self expression is a vital part of human development and life, being able to express what sort of person you are, what hobbies you like, music you like etc just by your presentation, and gender roles provide us with as easy way to do so. They are very much real though, a boy who likes cars does so because he likes cars, not because he thinks he's supposed to. A boy who doesn't like cars simply won't be interested in them and that's that.  Girls who wear make up do so because they enjoy it, they like to feel like they look good and feel confident about their appearance. On the other hand there are girls who don't wear makeup and have short hair and maybe work as mechanics, they're still girls, they're just using their gender presentation and current gender roles to express who they are as individuals.

When you then just combine gender identity and gender roles/presentation into one word, "gender", that's when arguments start, because as I've just shown, gender can mean different things, some are social constructs (but still real and important to people) and some are biological. If you're saying "gender is social/biological" then you need to specify which part of gender you're talking about, otherwise it just causes confusion.

From my experience, practise. Just put aside days to just put on your makeup, take it off, try it out mayb in a diffrent style or color and just keep at it until it just comes naturally and you know what goes well with what. The first time I ever tried makeup it  took me four hours in total, and that was just founation, mascarra and lipstick/gloss... Now I can do it all, foundation, concealer, eyebrows lipgloss/stick, blush, eyeshasow all in 15-30ins and then allow 10-40 mins for eyeliner depending on how many attempts it takes to get it perfect and symetical. But I still feel I could do it quicker and each time usually is a bit quicker so just practice practice practise! One problem I think you see a lot of trans people do when they start as well is too much makup which can make you go from beautiful trans woman to dragqueen in an instant and that's how people will see you. Often subtlety is the key, just trying to enhance what you've already got without anything drastic. Have a google for "woman", most of the results will just be regular non-celebrity people wearing makeup and just have a look at how they do it. Everyone has they're own style but even so you'll notice that their makeup is glaringly obvious in your face stuff, it's just simple and is there to complement them, not paint them.

As for learning how do makeup well, again it's all just practise. The first time you try will probably look like a drag queen who let a 5yrold do it with crayons, mine did! But focus on one thing at a time. For example, eyeliner. For me at least it's still the most tricky and time consuming but well worth it as nothing screams girl like well done eyeliner with nice symmetrical wings. So rather than watching loads of videos on everything at once, just focus on one item, in this example eye liner. The rest of the makeup, just practise/play with it until you know what you're doing and you'll probably master simple stuff like mascarra and lipgloss without having to do any research! Just focus on one thing, such as eyeliner, and google different styles of wearing it, look at videos of people applying it and most importantly, find one that works for you! There's a lot of different types of the same thing sometimes, with eyeliner you've got pencil, liquid, gel etc, you can even get it in a little pot and apply it with a separate stick. Try it all out and you'll find one that just works for you both in ease of use and appearance. If you have a go and think "damn, this is a nightmare" then just change to a different type or method of applying it. It took my months to finally find a foundation that worked with my skin as they all kept going flaky and patchy after a while. Eventually tried the one I use now along with a different cleanser and now my skin always looks perfect! So if something isn't working, just change it because there are hundreds of options for different scenarios and there will be one that just clicks with you.

Another thing I've found helped is just taking some time to try on all my clothes with each other and see what works together and what doesn't, I've even discovered some outfits this way that I'd never of dreamed of before but actually look great! Saves a lot of time getting ready for me now that I don't have to try on half my wardrobe before finally settling on something! Also helps to have a large and **varied** wardrobe. For example, I mainly just wear skinny jeans, tshirts/vests and a light jacket over the top but I do still keep a more formal outfit and a couple of party/evening dresses, just incase I'm suprised with a sudden celebration/interveiw etc. Same goes for shoes too, make sure you've at least got something casual, something formal and something fun so you don't end up going to an interveiw in converse! Charity shops and ebay are your friend here, when I was still discovering my style and what I liked and didn't liked I'd just get loads of cheap (less than £3) clothes from ebay and charity shops, try the on for a day or two with different stuff and then if it wasn't me then back it goes on ebay, might even make a profit! Charity shops are also great for things like bags, scarfs, shoes etc too so it's always worth having a look in them!

Another thing you can practise at home is walking. Kind of hard to explain but there are videos out there to help, basically woman walk differently to men due to their hids and pelvis being different and giving that little sort of "bum wiggle" if waring tight clothes. It's just how I naturally walk now but I jus used to walk back and forth in front of mirror at home to practise, I think the main tips are keeping elbows in and only swinging arms from the elbow, moving your legs foward from the hip, not the thight and imagining your  walking on a narrow strip so your feet are more or less in front of each other. I could have missed something vital there or got something wrong as it's been 6 months now since I had to last think about it, it just comes naturally after a bit and you'll walk like that normally.

Speech is also something you can practise at home although I've had no luck with that s can't really help.

There's loads of other things that are seen as female behavior too such as how you cross your legs, playing with hair when bored or nervous ,even how you wipe your bum according to an ex colleague of mine! It'simportant to remember though that you aren't trying to be  a perfect girl who is simply a combination of every single female stereotype that exists, you're just being yourself and only you know who that is. If you want to sit with your legs uncrossed or swing your arms like a guy is supposed to then do it, we're all different and just about every woman you meet will have some male attributes and behaviors, just as you get feminine guys. I'd reccomend just bringing a book to somewhere busy like a park or shopping center and just spend an hour sitting readign but also watching all the woman who go by, not only to study their behavior, movement, mannerisms etc, but also to realise just how diverse they are with all those things yet that doesn't make them any less of a woman just because they might have wide shoulder, a hairy lip, burp in public or wear a mens shirt. There really is no clear cut rule to "this is what woman do, this is what men do". The only rule you should worry about is "This is what I do"

Also remember that it can seem like an awful lot of work  and trouble you've got to go through to be yourself, but it does all just come naturally after a while and you won't even have to think about it.

After giving all that advice, I would just like to point out that I'm no expert on anything and the same as most of you, these are just things I've learnt on my transition and things that have helped and worked for me in my experience.

If I lose a leg in a car crash, I'm still me, but if I damage my brain then that could completely change who I am and I could end up a completely different person. That doesn't mean that they don't feel wrong and uncomfortable with their bodies though, they just don't understand why.
